newsitem.title: BRAZIL: COCOA - Bahia farmers sceptical over govt loans.
newsitem.headline: COCOA - Bahia farmers sceptical over govt loans.

text.p: Bahia cocoa farmers and traders said they were starting to doubt that 120 million Real worth of much-needed credits promised for farmers this year would ever be released by the government.

The loans, intended to help cash-strapped producers finance better crop husbandry, were promised at the start of the year but are taking even longer than to materialise than last year, when farmers only began to receive the cash in September.
"We hear new promises almost every day. One day they say it is with the BNDES (National Development Bank), then we hear it's gone to the Central Bank, and so on," one farmer complained.
"The last thing we heard was that it was with the Banco do Brasil."
One dealer speculated that the government may think it had done enough by abolishing a 13 percent sales tax known as ICMS, levied at state level, on cocoa destined for export.
The measure came into effect in October and the benefits to farmers have been increased by a rise in world prices.
"The government are probably thinking that the with the lifting of the ICMS tax, farmers have seen prices rise from 15 Real to nearly 20 Real so what more do they want," said a trader.
"It is possible that in the government there are people who think like that," added a farmer.

"The government has people who think in all kinds of ways. It is full of technocrats and bureaucrats who don't understand the Brazilian reality. Brazil is a huge country with complex problems but all the decisions are taken in a small place called Brasilia, which is an island of fantasy."
Farmers claimed that even with the higher prices, they were still not getting enough to be able to invest in productivity.
"The new price still does not make it worthwhile being a cocoa farmer," said one. "And in any case, there's no cocoa. What's the point of having a good price if you don't have the product to sell?"
Although last year's loans had come late and had only benefited around half of the producers who had applied for them, they had still been of use in fighting witch's broom disease, farmers said.
"If you follow the measures recommended by Ceplac (the govnerment's cocoa agency), they help a lot," said cocoa farmer Ronaldo Monteiro.
"I followed their instructions on my farms and I hardly had any trouble with witch's broom."
Internal prices remained at around 19.50 Real per 15-kilo arroba this week.
Farmers said that although a drought which wrecked the current main crop had ended two months ago, rainfall was still less than normal and soil moisture continued low.
The October-April main crop is expected to total only between 1.0 million and 1.1 million 60-kilo bags. Until a few years ago, Bahia traditionally produced main crops of around 3.0 million bags.
